messages.subject: Using SPDE from Lindgren et al. (2011)
parts:
Hello,

 I have some questions on using the spatial prediction methodology found in “An explicit link between Gaussian fields and Gaussian Markov random fields: The SPDE approach.” I will refer to this paper as ‘the jrssb paper.’

I’ve placed my questions in the comments in the code below. I’ve also summarized my questions at the end.

 

#I’m not sure if I’m running into problems in first three parts of my code. It is not #clear to me that the Delaunay triangulation is working. I’ve noticed that the #Delaunay triangulation needs to be defined in such a way that its’ borders #extend outside the borders of the spatial domain of interest. How does this #work for global prediction?

##########Part 1: the spatial locations

## The variable locs.full contains the spatial locations we would like to predict #at. It is an m by 2 vector #of coordinates.

# The variable obs contains the spatial locations we have observed data at. It is #an n by 2 vector of #coordinates.

 

locs.full<-read.table("locs_full.csv",sep = ",")

obs<-read.table("obs.csv",sep = ",")

 

    ## ################################

    ## Part 2: Covariates for the fixed effect term

    ## ################################

# X is an n times p matrix.

                X = read.table("covariates.csv",sep = ",")

    ## ################################

    ## Part 3: Delaunay triangulation

    ## ################################

 

    mesh = inla.mesh.create(

    loc=locs.full, ## optional

    cutoff=10/earth.radius,

    refine=list(max.edge=500/earth.radius))

 

    nmesh = mesh$n

    mesh.idx = mesh$idx$loc

 

############Part 4: The SPDE object

#The three lines of code indicated by items 1, 2, and 3 are not included and #commented out. They are meant to be a similar approach to modeling as #presented in Section 3.2 of the jrssb paper and the example in Section 4 #(however using b-splines in place of spherical harmonics).

    #item 1: basis.T <-inla.mesh.basis(mesh, type="b.spline", n=2, degree=2)

    # item 2: basis.K <-inla.mesh.basis(mesh, type="b.spline", n=2, degree=2)

#If using items (1) and (2) the spde object is specified as,

# item 3: spde = inla.spde.create(mesh = mesh, model = "matern", param=list(basis.K=basis.K, #basis.T=basis.T))

#I’ve left out items (1), (2) and (3) for two reasons: it is not clear to me that this #produces predictions similar to the example in Section 4 of the jrssb,  and #SPDE becomes slow as one includes more paramers.

# Since I am not sure the spde object in item 3 in the comments above give an #analysis similar to Section 4 of the jrssb paper I’ve been using the following #line.

spde = inla.spde.create(mesh = mesh, model = "matern", param=list(alpha=2))

                 field = c(rep(mesh.idx,1))

#When looking at the Cameletti et al. paper it appears that this gives a modeling approach similar to Sections 1 and 2 of the jrssb paper (i.e., precisions are based on Main Result 2 in Section 2.3). Is that #correct?

 

###########Part 5: Predictions using SPDE#########################

z = data.frame(data)

field = c(rep(mesh.idx,1))

formula <- (z ~ X + f(field, model = spde))

  

result = inla(formula, data = z , family = "gaussian")

fhat = result$summary.random$field[,"mean"]

beta_m1 = result$summary.fixed[,"mean"]

mu_m1 = X%*%beta_m1

Yhat = fhat[mesh.idx]+ mu_m1

 

# The result object appears to be giving approximate posterior distributions #based on INLA. However, I’m not sure what the prior specifications are, and I #need to report exactly what they are. Is there an equation line in the #references, or some default option that I can report?

 

So to summarize my questions,

(a)    (a) Does the specification of the Delaunay triangulation look standard or correct? If not or if you don't have enough information, what resources are available so I use a standard choice for the Delaunay triangulation.

(b)   (b) How does one change the code so that the Delaunay triangulation does not extend outside the borders of the globe? Does that go against the methodology if I choose not to extend outside the borders of the globe?

(c)    (c) Do items (1), (2), and (3) produce predictions similar to Section 4 of the jrssb paper? If not or if you don't have enough information, what resources are available so I can produce similar predictions.

(d)   (d) How many parameters are reasonable to include for spatial prediction using this SPDE approach?

(e)   (e) Will the uncommented spde object provide predictions similar to Sections 1 and 2 of the jrssb paper?

(f)     (f) Exactly what priors are being used?

 

I realize I’ve asked quite a few questions, and I don’t expect all to be answered. I’d appreciate any help! Thanks!


-Jon

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: Using SPDE from Lindgren et al. (2011)
parts: Answers below; some interleaved with your code, some at the end.
On Thursday, 13 September 2012 14:23:44 UTC+1, Jon wrote:

## The variable locs.full contains the spatial locations we would like to predict #at. It is an m by 2 vector #of coordinates.

# The variable obs contains the spatial locations we have observed data at. It is #an n by 2 vector of #coordinates.

Since elsewhere it's clear that you want to have a model on a sphere, the above indicates to me that you have supplied your coordinates as (longitude, latitude), or some other planar mapping of the sphere.
Proper models on a globe require correct topology and distance metric (very obvious close to the poles, not so obvious/required if all data are near the equator). For this reason, the meshing code in inla can build meshes of the sphere itself, when the user supplies the cartesian 3D-coordinates of the locations.  To do this, convert your (lon,lat) points to (x,y,z):

First, convert the lon,lat to radians (multiply by 180/pi), and then construct the cartesian coordinates through

loc = cbind(cos(lat)*cos(lon), cos(lat)*sin(lon), sin(lat))

Feeding this M-by-3 matrix into inla.mesh.create produces a meshed version of a unit radius sphere.

The output verctor from inla() can then be projected back onto a regular lon-lat-lattice, if needed for plotting purposes, say, with the inla.mesh.project and inla.mesh.projector functions.

> #I’ve left out items (1), (2) and (3) for two reasons: it is not clear to me that this #produces predictions similar to the example in > Section 4 of the jrssb,  and #SPDE becomes slow as one includes more paramers.
Those lines of code construct a non-stationary field model, where the parameters of the spde are allowed to vary slowly with latitude.
spde = inla.spde.create(mesh = mesh, model = "matern", param=list(alpha=2))
This produces a stationary field model.

#When looking at the Cameletti et al. paper it appears that this gives a modeling approach similar to Sections 1 and 2 of the jrssb paper (i.e., precisions are based on Main Result 2 in Section 2.3). Is that #correct?
Yes.

# The result object appears to be giving approximate posterior distributions #based on INLA. However, I’m not sure what the prior specifications are, and I #need to report exactly what they are. Is there an equation line in the #references, or some default option that I can report?

The prior for the spde model can be seen in
  spde$f$hyper.default
and by default the priors are Gaussian.  In particular for the newer spde models produced by inla.spde2.matern, the priors are chosen heuristically to match the spatial scale of the mesh domain, but for inla.spde.create the user can set them manually.
In both cases, the user can override the defaults by supplying a "hyper" parameter to the f()-function in the formula.

For all other parts of inla models, the default priors are listed in the output from inla.models(), e.g.
 inla.models()$latent$rw2$hyper

as well as in the documentation on http://www.r-inla.org/models

(a)    (a) Does the specification of the Delaunay triangulation look standard or correct? If not or if you don't have enough information, what resources are available so I use a standard choice for the Delaunay triangulation.

See my comments above.  The specific settings needed for inla.mesh.create are problem-dependent, and so requires more specific information for me to tell.  I am working on a tutorial text that will include some general guidelines for this.

(b)   (b) How does one change the code so that the Delaunay triangulation does not extend outside the borders of the globe? Does that go against the methodology if I choose not to extend outside the borders of the globe?
See above; "outside the globe" is not an issue when the mesh is build on the actual globe surface!

(c)    (c) Do items (1), (2), and (3) produce predictions similar to Section 4 of the jrssb paper? If not or if you don't have enough information, what resources are available so I can produce similar predictions.
Again, this is problem dependent.  The question has to begin with what kind of *model* is wanted/needed.
(d)   (d) How many parameters are reasonable to include for spatial prediction using this SPDE approach?

The number of parameters influences the speed and memory requirements for parameter estimation, which for spatial models can be substantial for non-stationary models.  The largest models I've run used around 18 parameters and 20 times 16000 mesh nodes, but I wouldn't recommend you to try that unless you really need it, and understand the underlying non-stationary models. 
There are several general options in inla to simplify the full Bayesian inference, allowing more complex models to run in shorter time, such as Empirical Bayes, and using Gaussian approximations without skewness corrections, and so on.
(e)   (e) Will the uncommented spde object provide predictions similar to Sections 1 and 2 of the jrssb paper?
That depends on how you use it in your model, i.e. it is problem-dependent.
(f)     (f) Exactly what priors are being used?

See above.

 
/Finn
